# Recursive Carry

Recursive replacement tells us that changing the boundary changes the state
domain.

But that raises a new question:

> **What happens to a completed realization when it is read from the enclosing
> boundary?**

R<sup>2</sup>D calls that change in count meaning **recursive carry**.

Recursive carry is not the physical transport of a state from one scale to
another.

It is not the accumulation of subordinate processes into a larger cause.

It is not reverse causation.

It is **boundary-relative reclassification**.

> **A completed local realization can acquire a different count meaning when
> the count boundary changes.**

[Recursive Replacement →](recursive-replacement.qmd)

## Begin With a Completed Local Realization

Consider a peer boundary

$$
B_{n,\alpha}.
$$

At that boundary, a completed local closure might be readable as

$$
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}:
i \rightarrow k \rightarrow i.
$$

The local states are readable.

The peer identity is readable.

The internal path is readable.

The realization therefore has a well-defined local count meaning at
\(B_{n,\alpha}\).

Now change to the enclosing boundary

$$
B_{n+1}.
$$

The local path is no longer necessarily readable as the same macrostate
sequence.

The enclosing boundary has its own state domain and its own classification.

The completed local realization must therefore be counted differently.

That is recursive carry.

## The Enclosing Occurrence Comes First Causally

Suppose the enclosing boundary contains a readable transition class

$$
\chi_{n+1}:
j \rightarrow k.
$$

Let one realized occurrence of that enclosing transition be

$$
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
$$

The enclosing occurrence can be locally realized through compatible closures
among its subordinate peer boundaries:

$$
\left\{
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\right\}_{\alpha\in I_n}.
$$

The causal relation is therefore

$$
\boxed{
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
\Longrightarrow
\left\{
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\right\}_{\alpha\in I_n}
}
$$

The enclosing occurrence defines which combinations of local realizations are
compatible with it.

The subordinate realizations are necessary for the enclosing occurrence to be
locally expressed.

But they do not independently combine to create the enclosing occurrence.

> **The whole defines its compatible realizations.**

[The Causal Inversion →](causal-inversion.qmd)

## Carry Points the Other Way — But It Is Not a Causal Arrow

Now select one completed local realization:

$$
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}.
$$

When the count boundary changes from \(B_n\) to \(B_{n+1}\), that completed
local realization is reclassified according to the enclosing occurrence to
which it belongs.

R<sup>2</sup>D denotes this as

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
}
$$

The symbol

$$
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
$$

means:

> **change in count meaning under change of boundary.**

It is not a dynamical arrow.

It does not mean

$$
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\Longrightarrow
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
$$

The causal relation runs the other way.

So R<sup>2</sup>D distinguishes two different questions.

### Causal realization

$$
\boxed{
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
\Longrightarrow
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
}
$$

asks:

> Which local realizations are compatible with this enclosing occurrence?

### Recursive carry

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
}
$$

asks:

> How is this completed local realization classified when the count boundary
> changes?

The arrows point in opposite diagrammatic directions.

They do not describe opposite causal flows.

## Carry Is Reclassification

This is the simplest way to think about recursive carry.

At the local boundary:

$$
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
$$

has local closure meaning.

At the enclosing boundary:

$$
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
$$

has enclosing occurrence meaning.

The two are not the same boundary-defined state object.

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\not\equiv
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
}
$$

as count objects.

Recursive carry does not preserve one unchanged state across the boundary.

Instead:

> **local state identity is replaced while the recursive relation remains
> consequential.**

This is why carry follows naturally from recursive replacement.

Replacement changes the state domain.

Carry tells us how a completed realization is counted after that change.

## A Coin Example

Consider one coin at a subordinate boundary.

A local realization might complete a cycle such as

$$
H \rightarrow T \rightarrow H.
$$

At that boundary, the sequence is readable.

The source coin is identifiable.

The path is identifiable.

Now suppose many such subordinate coin boundaries participate in an
enclosing ensemble.

At the ensemble boundary, the question is no longer:

> Which exact coin followed which exact path?

The enclosing state may instead classify the completed subordinate
realizations according to an ensemble occurrence.

Different local histories can therefore acquire the same enclosing count
meaning.

Schematically:

$$
H\rightarrow T\rightarrow H
$$

and

$$
H\rightarrow T\rightarrow H
$$

for two different peer coins can both participate in the same enclosing
ensemble classification.

The local path identities remain meaningful at the subordinate boundaries.

But they need not remain recoverable as separate state identities from the
enclosing occurrence.

[The Coins Example →](coins.qmd)

## Carry Is Generally Many-to-One

Suppose two distinct local closures satisfy

$$
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\neq
\mathcal{C}_{n,\beta},
$$

but both are classified as realizations of the same enclosing occurrence:

$$
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
$$

and

$$
\mathcal{C}_{n,\beta}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
$$

Then the enclosing occurrence does not uniquely specify which local path
occurred.

Schematically,

$$
\boxed{
\left|
\kappa_n^{-1}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
\right)
\right|
>
1
}
$$

More than one locally distinguishable realization belongs to the same
enclosing classification.

This is a central feature of recursive carry.

> **Carry can preserve count consequence while removing recoverable local
> path identity.**

## The Local Path Is Not Destroyed

Many-to-one carry does not mean the subordinate path ceased to exist.

The path remains definable at the boundary where it was readable.

What changes is whether that identity can be reconstructed from the enclosing
state.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{local readability}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{enclosing recoverability}
}
$$

The subordinate realization remains real at its own boundary.

But the enclosing boundary does not have to preserve its full path identity.

This is another reason R<sup>2</sup>D differs from a picture in which one
fixed microscopic ontology is carried unchanged through every scale.

## One Enclosing Occurrence Can Organize Many Peers

An enclosing occurrence generally involves multiple subordinate peer
boundaries.

Thus,

$$
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
\Longrightarrow
\left\{
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\right\}_{\alpha\in I_n}.
$$

If the peers are equivalent under the enclosing compatibility relation, one
peer may sometimes be selected as a **representative peer**.

That does not mean the representative peer generates the enclosing
occurrence.

Nor is it necessarily an average over all peers.

It is simply one local realization representative of a class of equivalent
peer relations under the same enclosing organization.

If the peer boundaries are not equivalent, the peer index must remain
explicit.

No representative-peer reduction is then assumed.

## Carry Does Not Mean "The Parts Build the Whole"

This distinction is important because recursive diagrams are easy to read
bottom-up.

One might imagine:

$$
\text{local closure}
+
\text{local closure}
+
\text{local closure}
\rightarrow
\text{enclosing occurrence}.
$$

That is not the R<sup>2</sup>D causal architecture.

The enclosing occurrence defines which local closures are jointly compatible
with it.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{enclosing occurrence}
\Longrightarrow
\text{compatible subordinate closures}.
}
$$

Only after a subordinate realization is completed do we ask how that
realization is **read from the enclosing boundary**.

That is carry.

The distinction is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{organization downward}
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\text{classification across boundaries}.
}
$$

Not:

$$
\text{causation upward}
+
\text{causation downward}.
$$

## Carry Is Not Physical Transport

Nothing must physically travel from \(B_n\) into \(B_{n+1}\).

The boundary changes.

The classification changes.

The same recursively organized relation is now read differently.

This is why the notation

$$
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
$$

should not be interpreted as:

- motion;
- energy flow;
- information flow;
- force transmission;
- or transport between scales.

It denotes a formal operation:

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary-relative reclassification}.
}
$$

## Carry Is Not a Dynamical Evolution Operator

A dynamical operator ordinarily maps one state into another within a state
space.

Recursive carry does something different.

It changes the state space from which the realization is being classified.

Thus,

$$
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
$$

does not mean that the local closure dynamically evolves into the enclosing
occurrence.

It means that the completed local realization has enclosing occurrence
meaning when the boundary changes.

This is why recursive carry belongs to the architecture of counting before it
belongs to any particular physical dynamics.

## Carry and Replacement

Recursive replacement and recursive carry are closely related but distinct.

### Recursive replacement

$$
\boxed{
\text{change of boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{change of state domain}
}
$$

The old state classification does not persist unchanged.

### Recursive carry

$$
\boxed{
\text{completed local realization}
\rightarrow
\text{new enclosing count meaning}
}
$$

The realized relation is reclassified at the new boundary.

So:

> **Replacement changes what the states are.**

> **Carry changes what a completed realization counts as.**

[Recursive Replacement →](recursive-replacement.qmd)

## Carry and Closure

Recursive carry becomes especially clear when the local relation has closed.

A local closure might be

$$
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}:
i \rightarrow k \rightarrow i.
$$

The local state returns.

The path is complete relative to that boundary.

That completed relation can then be classified from the enclosing boundary
without requiring its internal path identity to remain readable there.

Closure therefore provides a natural unit of completed local realization for
recursive carry.

[Closure →](closure.qmd)

## Carry and Recurrence Are Different

A completed local closure may recur many times.

An enclosing occurrence may recur at another count rate.

Recursive carry does not assert that these recurrence counts are equal.

It states only the compatibility and reclassification relation between the
boundary-specific reads.

The relative recurrence between adjacent boundaries is a separate count
relation.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{carry}
\neq
\text{recurrence ratio}.
}
$$

[Recurrence →](recurrence.qmd)

## Carry and Irreversibility Are Different

Recursive carry must also be separated from irreversibility.

A completed local closure can return to its initial state while the opposed
legs of the closure are realized with unequal occurrence-count efficiency.

That is a question of local nonreciprocity.

Recursive carry asks a different question:

> How is the completed realization classified when the boundary changes?

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{recursive carry}
=
\text{cross-boundary reclassification}
}
$$

while

$$
\boxed{
\text{occurrence-count loss}
=
\text{local directional nonreciprocity}.
}
$$

The two should not be conflated.

In particular, recursive carry does not require a special "surviving
fraction" of a local realization to be selected before it can be carried.

Nor does carry divide the local realization into separate upward directed and
background channels.

The relationship between local occurrence-count nonreciprocity and enclosing
background belongs to the R<sup>2</sup>D Second Law, not to the definition of
carry.

[The R²D Second Law →](second-law.qmd)

## The Two-Sided Recursive Architecture

For every nonterminal boundary, R<sup>2</sup>D therefore contains two
complementary relations.

### Enclosing definition of local realization

$$
\boxed{
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
\Longrightarrow
\left\{
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\right\}
}
$$

The whole defines which local realizations are compatible with it.

### Boundary-relative reclassification

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
}
$$

The completed local realization acquires enclosing count meaning when the
boundary changes.

These are not a causal cycle.

They are two readings of one recursive relation.

> **The enclosing relation defines its compatible local realizations.  
> Recursive carry changes how those completed realizations are counted across
> boundaries.**

## Why Carry Matters

Recursive carry supplies the bridge between neighboring state domains without
requiring one fixed object to persist through them.

It explains how:

- subordinate realizations can remain consequential after their state
  identities are replaced;
- many distinct local histories can belong to one enclosing state;
- an enclosing occurrence can be represented through local realizations
  without being caused by their independent accumulation;
- and the same recursively organized relation can have different readable
  forms at adjacent boundaries.

This is the architecture required before the R<sup>2</sup>D law can relate
local closure and enclosing occurrence.

[The R²D Law →](r2d-law.qmd)

## The Core Distinction

The entire idea can be summarized in three statements:

> **Recursive replacement:** the state domain changes.

> **Causal realization:** the enclosing relation defines its compatible local
> realizations.

> **Recursive carry:** a completed local realization acquires a new count
> meaning when the boundary changes.

Or schematically:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ccc}
& \chi_{n+1}^{(r)} & \\
& \Downarrow & \\
& \mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha} &
\end{array}
}
$$

for causal realization, while

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
}
$$

denotes reclassification.

The first is causal.

The second is not.

That distinction is essential to R<sup>2</sup>D.
